source: van Ravenzwaaij, Boekel, Forstmann, Ratcliff, Wagenmakers (2014) Action video games do not improve the speed of information processing in simple perceptual tasks
finding: Gap 8. Two supervised training experiments tried to replicate the claim that action games speed up information processing. Action gamers, cognitive gamers (Tetris-type game) and non-gamers all showed the same practice effects.
numbers: Exp 1: N=20 students, 10 per condition, 5 supervised sessions. Exp 2: N=45, 15 per condition (action, cognitive, no-game control), six days. Action game Unreal Tournament 2004. Mean RT speed-up first to last session 51 ms (action) vs 59 ms (cognitive). Session x condition interactions had Bayes factors BF01 of about 2 to 10 in favour of the null.
quote: playing action video games does not improve the speed of information processing in simple perceptual tasks
limits: Small cells (10 to 15 per group) but with Bayes factors and an active control. Participants screened for little prior gaming. Only a simple perceptual task; short training (5 sessions).
agent_relevance: A narrow trained skill gives practice gains that an unrelated game also gives. Compare a scaffold against an active control, not a no-scaffold baseline.

source: Unsworth, Redick, McMillan, Hambrick, Kane, Engle (2015) Is playing video games related to cognitive abilities?
finding: Gap 8. Extreme-groups comparison showed gamers beat non-gamers, but across the full range of subjects, at task level and latent level, nearly all relations were near zero.
numbers: Two experiments; working memory, fluid intelligence and attention-control measures plus a gaming questionnaire. Exact N and latent correlations NOT obtained (full text blocked, HTTP 403); only the abstract was read through Europe PMC.
limits: Abstract only. Critiqued in 'Playing Some Video Games but Not Others Is Related to Cognitive Abilities' (2017, Psychological Science, doi 10.1177/0956797616644837), which argues genre and measurement matter.
agent_relevance: Extreme-group contrasts inflate effects; a gain seen between good and poor prompts or scaffolds may vanish in a full-range analysis.

source: Owen et al. (2010) Putting brain training to the test (Nature)
finding: Gap 10. Independent, very large online trial: six weeks of training improved every trained task but gave no transfer, even to closely related tasks.
numbers: N=11,430 participants; training several times per week for six weeks on reasoning, memory, planning, visuospatial and attention tasks.
limits: Not preregistered; online, uncontrolled setting. Older than the Sala and Gobet analyses.
agent_relevance: Large-N evidence from a group outside Sala and Gobet that task practice does not give general gains.

source: Simons, Boot, Charness, Gathercole, Chabris, Hambrick, Stine-Morrow (2016) Do brain-training programs work? (Psychological Science in the Public Interest)
finding: Gap 10. Independent comprehensive review with stated best practices for training studies, written to settle two conflicting consensus letters.
numbers: Letters: one from more than 70 scientists (no evidence of benefit) and a counter-letter from 133 scientists and practitioners. Only the abstract was read; the review's verdict figures were not read.
limits: Abstract only. Not a new data set.
agent_relevance: Gives a checklist (active control, preregistration, outcomes not tied to the training task) to apply to our scaffold ablations.

source: Gobet and Sala (2023) Cognitive training: a field in search of a phenomenon
finding: Gap 10. Latest summary by the Sala and Gobet group: the far-transfer effect is null and there is little true variability between training types. Remaining apparent effects are sampling error and artifacts.
numbers: No new data; summarises second-order meta-analyses and answers Green et al. 2019.
limits: Same research group as most nulls in K01, so not independent. Position paper.
agent_relevance: Treat K01 as strong for humans but note that one group dominates the synthesis.

source: Sala and Gobet (2019 preprint) Working memory training in typically developing children: a multilevel meta-analysis
finding: Gap 10. Near transfer is small to medium and proportional to task similarity; far transfer is null once active controls are used.
numbers: m=41 studies, k=393 effects, N=2,375. Far transfer with active controls: g=0.001, SE=0.055, p=.982, tau2=0.000.
limits: Same group as d05. Children only. Preprint version, abstract read.
agent_relevance: Near transfer scales with similarity of trained and test tasks: use as a design rule for held-out tests.

source: Foroughi, Monfort, Paczynski, McKnight, Greenwood (2016) Placebo effects in cognitive training (PNAS)
finding: Gap 10. Boundary condition from the other side: a suggestive recruitment flyer produced apparent gains after one hour of training.
numbers: Self-selected placebo group showed a gain equal to 5 to 10 IQ points after a single 1-h session; controls responding to a neutral flyer showed none.
limits: Small study, abstract read; a later attempt (d08) found no expectancy effect.
agent_relevance: Uncontrolled expectation can fake transfer; for LLMs the analogue is judge or prompt-framing bias.

source: (Un)Great expectations: the role of placebo effects in cognitive training (2018, Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition)
finding: Gap 10. An attempt to induce expectancy effects in n-back training found none, in either direction.
numbers: Trained n-back improved regardless of induced expectation; expectation gave no gains in the active control group. Sample sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only; author list not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Placebo explanations do not fully remove training effects, but those effects stay near transfer.

source: Kim, Yang, Jung (2024) Persona is a double-edged sword: mitigating the negative impact of role-playing prompts in zero-shot reasoning (arXiv 2408.08631)
finding: Gap 2. Tested persona prompts on larger closed models (GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo) plus Llama3-8B across 12 reasoning sets. Persona helps on average with GPT-4 but hurts some items and datasets; Llama3 got worse on 7 of 12 sets.
numbers: GPT-4 arithmetic average: base 91.06, persona 92.28, Jekyll and Hyde ensemble 93.15 (AQuA 68.24 to 74.80 with persona). GPT-4 other-task average: base 61.37, persona 77.08 (Letter 19.80 to 92.80, Date 66.93 to 75.93; Strategy 76.42 to 75.71 and Object 79.22 to 78.41, both down). Llama3-8B other-task average persona 74.49 vs base 74.68. AQuA confusion matrix (Llama3): persona right and base wrong 13.78%, persona wrong and base right 15.75%.
limits: Personas are task-matched and the big Letter gain may come from instruction or format rather than expertise. No Claude or Gemini. Gains concentrated in a few datasets.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 2: with GPT-4 a persona is not harmful on average and helps on a few tasks, but it flips right answers to wrong on about 16% of AQuA items for a small model. Use a neutral-versus-persona check, not a fixed persona.

source: Chu et al. (2025) SFT memorizes, RL generalizes (arXiv 2501.17161, ICML)
finding: Gap 4. In GeneralPoints (card arithmetic) and V-IRL (navigation), outcome-reward RL improved on rule variants never seen; SFT fell on the same variants. SFT still helps RL by stabilising output format.
numbers: Out-of-distribution rule variant: RL GP-L 11.5 to 15.0 (+3.5), V-IRL-L 80.8 to 91.8 (+11.0); SFT GP-L 11.5 to 3.4 (-8.1), V-IRL-L 80.8 to 1.3 (-79.5). Visual: RL GP-VL 23.6 to 41.2, V-IRL-VL 16.7 to 77.8; SFT 23.6 to 13.7 and 16.7 to 11.1. V-IRL mini benchmark 44.0 to 77.8.
limits: Two synthetic tasks and rule changes only; the SFT collapse of -79.5 points is partly format breakage.
agent_relevance: Mechanism part 1: RL on outcomes keeps general abilities, SFT on fixed traces overfits format. A prompt scaffold changes no weights, so it should sit closer to RL in this respect (see d11).

source: Shenfeld, Pari, Agrawal (2025) RL's Razor: why online RL forgets less (arXiv 2509.04259)
finding: Gap 4. Forgetting is predicted by how far the fine-tuned policy moves from the base policy, measured as forward KL on the new task. On-policy RL is biased toward small-KL solutions; SFT can land arbitrarily far.
numbers: Quadratic fit of forgetting vs forward KL: R2=0.961 (ParityMNIST), R2=0.71 for the LLM experiments. An oracle SFT distribution built to minimise KL forgot even less than RL. Other candidate predictors (weight change, representation shift, total variation) were weaker than forward KL.
limits: R2 is lower for LLMs than toy tasks; Qwen 2.5 3B to 14B and one robotics model only. Correlational for LLMs.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 mechanism: it is distribution shift, not RL as such. Prompt scaffolding changes no parameters so cannot cause this forgetting, but it can still shift output behaviour, which this paper does not test.

source: Liu et al. (2026, ICLR) SPIRAL: self-play on zero-sum games incentivizes reasoning (arXiv 2506.24119 v3), Table 1 and appendix ablations
finding: Gap 5. Part of the gain from game training is generic: SFT on game trajectories also lifts reasoning scores, but self-play RL adds more. A single-game specialist already transfers. No non-game synthetic control was run.
numbers: Qwen3-4B-Base average 34.0: SFT-Kuhn 37.4, SFT-Multi 39.7 (25k and 52k trajectories both 39.7), SPIRAL-Kuhn 43.4, SPIRAL-Multi 44.5. Qwen3-8B 39.5: SFT-Multi 46.1, SPIRAL 49.6. Octothinker-8B 25.8: SFT 27.0, SPIRAL 33.8. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct 23.9: SFT 25.0, SPIRAL 25.9. Single-game SPIRAL: TicTacToe 41.3, Kuhn 43.4, Negotiation 40.0. Weak-opponent ablations: Mistral opponent 29.6, Gemini opponent 33.4 (both below base 34.0).
limits: Few-shot Qwen3 evaluation protocol; 8 benchmarks; SFT baseline may help through format as well as skill. Gains shrink for the instruction-tuned Llama (+2.0). Table text partly garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Share of gain matched by SFT on the same games: about 54% (5.7 of 10.5) for Qwen3-4B, 66% (6.6 of 10.1) for 8B, 15% for Octothinker. So much of the gain is exposure to game data and style; RL adds the rest. A fair test needs non-game synthetic tasks in the same format.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners (AAAI; arXiv 2308.10144)
finding: Gap 6. Retrieving past solved trajectories and extracted insights helps within a domain, and insights from HotpotQA carried over to FEVER, a different task. Experience diversity (success and failure pairs) mattered.
numbers: Transfer HotpotQA to FEVER success rate: ReAct baseline 58; ExpeL variants roughly 63 (no task demos), 65 and 70 (table layout garbled in extraction, assignment of 65 and 70 not certain). Retrieve-only with Reflexion on the main benchmark: 40.3% to 54.4% over rounds; with insights 54.5% to 60.4% and 59.0% to 64.2%.
limits: gpt-3.5 class agent; transfer is between closely related QA tasks, not novel problems. Does not test harm from retrieval on novel problems.
agent_relevance: Supports pattern memory on structured tasks. It does not test the random-position-chess analogue (patterns hurting on unstructured input), so gap 6 stays partly open.

source: Afonin et al. (2026) Emergent misalignment via in-context learning (arXiv 2510.11288 v4)
finding: Gap 9. Cross-domain contamination does occur at prompt level: narrow in-context examples (risky finance, bad extreme-sports advice, wrong facts) made models give misaligned answers to unrelated benign queries.
numbers: 4 model families (Gemini, Kimi-K2, Grok, Qwen). With 16 in-context examples EM rates were 1% to 24% depending on model and domain; effect appears with as few as 2 examples. Larger models typically more susceptible; reasoning mode gave marginally higher EM. With only 25% bad examples EM fell to about 1.6 to 0.4%. 67% of misaligned reasoning traces mention harm, danger or recklessness. GPT-4o vs human judge agreement 91 to 93%.
limits: Examples are deliberately harmful or wrong; rates are low outside the strongest cases. Prompt content is data context, not a clean domain module.
agent_relevance: Yes, it can happen at prompt level, so a domain module with flawed worked examples could leak style or bias across tasks. Keep module examples correct and run an unrelated-query check; an instruction to prioritise safety lowered EM.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR; arXiv 2310.01798)
finding: Gap 3. A generic verify-and-revise guardrail without outside feedback does not help reasoning and often hurts. It only helps when an oracle label says when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after self-correction (3 calls) and 41.8 (5 calls); GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0. With oracle labels GPT-4 GSM8K reached 97.5. GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: Table text partly garbled in extraction; GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama-2 era models, not reasoning models. Does not test a rule-restating guardrail on counterfactual twins.
agent_relevance: A verification step must bring new information (rule text, tool, test) to help. This does not answer gap 3 directly: rule restating has not been measured on Wu's twins.

source: Pfau, Merrill, Bowman (2024) Let's think dot by dot: hidden computation in transformer language models (arXiv 2404.15758)
finding: Gap 1. A length-matched placebo can capture much of a scaffold's benefit when models are trained to use it. Meaningless filler tokens replaced chain of thought on two hard algorithmic tasks.
numbers: 3SUM-type task: chain of thought 95.1%, filler 93.6%, no intermediate tokens 78.7%, majority-class baseline 63%. Another task: filler kept 100% while no-filler stayed near 66%. Small transformers trained from scratch.
limits: Synthetic tasks with dense supervision; learning to use filler was hard. Does not show that prompting an off-the-shelf model with filler helps.
agent_relevance: Argument for always including a length-matched placebo scaffold when testing held-out domains; compute alone can give part of a gain.
